extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, contributors and advanced students reading a 19th-century mathematical journal (problem-solvers and proof-writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Produce and present mathematical theorems, proofs, and exercise solutions in journal style: state problems/theorems clearly, define notation, apply transformations or geometric constructions, show computations, and include verification/corollaries. Emphasizes series manipulation, finite-difference transforms, tabulation-suitable reductions, and multiple solution methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct solution with explicit notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a direct solution by introducing clear notation for the figure and quantities (e.g. name triangle sides a, b, c; arcs from angles A,B,C to point O; angles subtended at O), then derive relations step by step (e.g. use cos(θ1+θ2)=cos θ2 to obtain known relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page's 'DIRECT SOLUTION OF A SPHERICAL PROBLEM' begins by letting a, b, c be sides, defining arcs and angles at O, and proceeds to replace trig quantities by their expressions in subdivided triangles to obtain a symmetric equation. Guidance: define all variables, reduce to known identities, and carry through algebraic substitutions to a neat final relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce multivariable integrals to single-variable functions suitable for tabulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible transform integrals or functions of several variables into functions of one variable to make them 'altogether suitable for tabulation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set tan t = 1/x and manipulate the integral sin a(α',a) into a difference of single-variable functions i^ (ω) — i^ (ω+α). Note the admonition that some integrals (e.g. 0i) may not admit similar reduction. Aim to obtain forms depending on a single variable before tabulating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and state practical convergence domains for series expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: When expanding functions into series, explicitly note the region of convergence and whether the resulting series are practically usable in the intended numerical regime (e.g. 'convergence will not be practically available unless x ≈ 1').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that certain series 'cannot be employed when the value of it approaches to unity' and that expansions may be 'ill suited to tabulation' if parameters make convergence poor. Always state the domain where the series method is valid and prefer alternative representations outside that domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sign and term-by-term considerations when expanding integrands
rubrics_metrics.description: When obtaining integrals by expanding functions (e.g. arctan, logarithms), track the signs and all terms carefully, as expansions include alternating signs and higher-power terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page obtains integrals 'by expanding the tan^(-1) and [the other function] ... (including their sign) — a? sin a — a?^2 2 — 2 sin 2a — ...' Advice: write out the series with sign, list the resulting trigonometric coefficient structure, and note when such series break down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use finite-difference and transform methods for summation and interpolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the algebraic-transformation/finite-difference framework: take successive orders of differences until they vanish, select the last term of each set (from a chosen portion), arrange quotients by factorial denominators in retrograde order, and apply multipliers to reconstruct sums or interpolate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horner's method (arts. 33–38) is given in detail: view a transformee table, interpret differences as derived functions, use DN, D^N notation, and connect to Taylor's theorem (infinitesimal differences). Practical recipe: pick I-term portion, take orders n, divide differences by 1,2,6,24..., arrange and apply virtual multipliers (w,n-1,...,1) and the remaining increment (α—I) to complete the series. Examples (Ex 1–3) illustrate computation of cubes, sums of cubes, and nth-term extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reductions to pure transformee where advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible reduce a problem to a 'pure transformee' (a simplified canonical transformed sequence) to take advantage of continuous approximation and to simplify later operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes the formula differs from the one now in use and 'possessing every advantage of the system of continuous approximation, and harmonising with the other parts of that system, it seems to merit a particular elucidation.' Use this reduction to simplify summation/interpolation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and use multiplier bookkeeping (digit-increments vs unit-increments)
rubrics_metrics.description: When doing stepwise numerical reconstruction of values from tables or series, clearly manage 'virtual multipliers' and the mode of increments (digit-increments vs unit-increments), since these determine the multipliers used at each course of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples explain virtual multipliers (4,3,2,1) and how digit-increments produce multipliers like 31,21,11,1; later contractions reduce order. Advice: plan increment strategy, compute appropriate multipliers, and reduce the operation order when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple independent solutions and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: For important problems give more than one solution (geometric, analytic, algebraic, projection, calculus) to illustrate different viewpoints, check correctness, and show broader applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many problems in the page are followed by 'First Solution', 'Second Solution', etc., e.g. the quadrilateral/circumcircle center problem and the moment-of-inertia problem. Each solution uses different tools (perpendicular bisectors, projection to ellipse, principal axes). Encouraged: present at least one synthetic/geometric and one analytic/computational approach where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include verification and consistency checks
rubrics_metrics.description: After deriving formulas or numeric results, give verification steps that connect the result to known values or alternative representations (e.g. equivalence to logarithms and their derivative functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts 'it deserves to be remarked, as a means of verification, that the formula just written is equivalent to log 314 and its derivative functions...' Use such cross-checks (limiting cases, known identities, comparing sums/columns to known sequences) to validate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure proofs with clear auxiliary constructions and stepwise deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: State theorem/problem clearly, define notation, draw or name auxiliary points/lines, derive stepwise relations using standard lemmas (inscriptible quadrilaterals, similar triangles, perpendicular bisectors), and conclude with the claimed result and corollaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proofs in the page consistently: label points (O, P, Q...), draw perpendiculars, invoke inscribed-angle or chord properties, deduce parallelism/perpendicularity and conclude. Theorem presentations often end with corollaries or remarks about limiting cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss parameter cases, limiting behavior, and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: When a solution depends on parameters or quantities that may vary (e.g. points in sides vs in sides produced, or angles approaching limits), explicitly discuss parameter ranges, limiting cases and state corollaries derived from the main result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the conic-through-six-points problem includes corollaries: when triangle sides are diminished or when points lie in sides produced; the tabulation discussion notes when series representation is unsuitable. Always identify and state special-case consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: For applied-mechanics quantities, give multiple computation approaches and show equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: For quantities like moments of inertia, present at least two approaches (principal-axes decomposition, projection to ellipse, direct integration), compute the same quantity and show the expressions coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moment-of-inertia problem is solved via principal axes (Poisson formula), projection to an ellipse and direct integration; all yield MA' = 1/2 π a^4 (1 + sin^2 α) (as in the page). Presenting multiple routes strengthens confidence and provides insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and exploit general theorems or universal precepts rather than ad hoc casework
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with diverse increments or special-case complications, rely on concise universal precepts or general theorems (e.g. the 'General Theorem' referenced) to handle many cases uniformly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises trusting the 'concise and universal precept of the General Theorem' to handle diverse increment schemes. Use general identities or theorems to avoid repetitive ad hoc manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record algebraic transformations and tabulate ordinal/derivative dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: When using algebraic transformation methods, tabulate relations among absolute terms and their differences (e.g. arrange DN, D^N,... rows) to make ordinal and derivative dependence explicit and to guide multiplication rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horner provides tabulations where marginal directions for multiplying are adapted to cases w≤n etc. Use tabulated difference arrays to determine multipliers and to understand derivative/dependence structure; this aids reduction to transformees and practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using series/tables for numerical logs or constants, introduce increments digit-by-digit with bookkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the entire numerical increment one digit at a time into the table/series, using contraction and reduction steps to manage computational order and maintain precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example for computing log(3.1415926536) uses digit-by-digit insertion into a table of logs from 1 to 1000, noting how virtual multipliers change course-by-course and how contractions reduce the operation order. Practically: plan digit insertion and contractions to control complexity.
